_note: The three-phase teach-a-word routine. The words themselves are not here: every article already carries two word-and-definition pairs as its vocabulary question, which is 700 of them across seven grades, each already tied to a grade and a standard. This file holds only the routine, in our own words. The structure of say-it, use-it, write-it is a common one -- Kate Kinsella's vocabulary work is the version most teachers have met -- and the script below is ours, not hers.
title: Teach a Word
blurb: Three phases, about ten minutes, one word. Say it, use it, write it.

steps.t: Say the word, then have them say it
steps.say: The word is {WORD}. Say it with me: {WORD}.
steps.do: Everybody says it out loud. Twice if it has more than two syllables.
Clap once per syllable. A word nobody can pronounce will not get used.

steps.t: Give the meaning in plain words
steps.do: They listen. Do not ask what it means yet — they have not met it.

steps.t: Use it in a sentence about them
steps.do: Make your sentence about this class, this room, today. An example about nobody is harder to copy.
A frame is the whole point of this phase. Without one the confident children answer and the rest stay quiet.

steps.say: Tell your partner your sentence. Use the word.
steps.do: Everybody says it to somebody. Walk and listen for a sentence to borrow in the next step.
Read a real sentence from the room. Name the child. This is the step that makes the next word worth trying.
Spelling matters less here than having written it once in their own hand.

steps.say: Write the sentence you just said.
steps.do: The one they already said out loud. Saying it first is what makes this quick.

steps.say: Draw the word, or circle it the next time you see it.
steps.do: A drawing for a thing, a mark for an idea. Not every word can be drawn and that is worth admitting.

placement._note: Where this sits in a lesson. Ten minutes on one word only pays off if the word comes back.
lines: Teach the word before the text it comes from, not after. The point is to clear it out of the way.
Two words a day is the ceiling. Four words taught properly beats ten mentioned.
Use the word yourself, out loud, three more times that week. If you do not use it again, neither will they.
The word is in an article's vocabulary question, so the article is the place it comes back.
